articles.body: Disclosure: I work on LaunchReach, which has guided SPF/DKIM/DMARC setup for sending from your own domain. It is mentioned near the end. The steps below work with any email provider. You have a launch coming. You have written the announcement and built a list. Before you hit send, there is one boring job that decides whether the email reaches inboxes or ends up in spam: authenticating your sending domain. Three DNS records do this: SPF, DKIM and DMARC. This is what each one does and how to check them, written for a founder who would rather not become a mail admin. The short version SPF lists which servers may send mail for your domain. DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to each message, so receivers can verify it was authorised by your domain and not altered.

Yet, if you look at how most modern "computer use" and desktop agents work under the hood, you will notice a glaring architectural tension. Most existing solutions attempt to interact with your operating system through the lens of a human: taking continuous screenshots, feeding them into multimodal vision models, computing pixel coordinates, and synthesizing artificial mouse clicks. While technically impressive as a proof of concept, this approach hits a hard wall when applied to serious systems engineering.

articles.title: \"Tests pass\" is a claim, not evidence — the receipt format I use to prove an agent's fix (red on old, green on new)
articles.excerpt: I commented on a thread this week about agent PR gates and kept circling the same gap: everyone agrees "no model grades the model," but when the agent says tests pass, what artifact proves it? The PR…
articles.body: I commented on a thread this week about agent PR gates and kept circling the same gap: everyone agrees "no model grades the model," but when the agent says tests pass , what artifact proves it? The PR description is just another claim. So I built the receipt half of the answer. Here's the format and the honest limits. The receipt: red on old, green on new The core idea is boring and that's why it works. Take your eval suite, run it twice: Before — on the pre-patch code. Save results as before.jsonl . After — on the patched code. Save as after.jsonl . Seal — hash both files + the suite name + the commit SHAs into one receipt JSON. Verify — anyone can recompute the hashes later and confirm the record wasn't edited after the fact. The receipt doesn't prove the tests are good — nothing can.

articles.excerpt: The longest total solar eclipse on land this century promises to be the experience of a lifetime, but watching it from Luxor, Egypt, may not be straightforward. What could go wrong? Quite a lot, actua…
articles.body: On Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view. I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong? I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of lightwhile observing Jupiter and its moon volcanic moon Io. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule.

articles.body: On Episode 237 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle sign off — temporarily — with a look at space news, a bushel of space jokes, and a recap of some of our funniest moments. Welcome to the last episode of This Week in Space . It's been a good run — including our betas, we produced about 240 episodes of the show, and had a blast doing it. We appreciate all of you, our fine listeners, for accompanying us on this journey, and are working to continue in a new venue in early 2027. To track our progress, and get your weekly fix of Rod's terrible space humor, find us on Instagram and Facebook: @rodandtariq Download or subscribe to this show at: https://twit.tv/shows/this-week-in-space .

articles.title: 'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest big-screen adventure
articles.excerpt: Assimilate this! How cyber-zombies and the "birth of 'Star Trek'" gave Jean-Luc Picard one of his finest hours.
articles.body: Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing , there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard . "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend.
articles.author: Richard Edwards

articles.title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
articles.excerpt: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public…
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.

articles.title: SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk says
articles.excerpt: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. Rather, it will go on display as a museum piece, according to company founder and CEO Elon Musk.
articles.body: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas. Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk , who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen. "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit .
